name: Black Fast

card.summary: The Black Fast is a traditional Christian fast with no food until after sunset and one simple evening meal, which people also treat as a time-restricted eating pattern that can lower intake and support a leaner look.
card.note: Originates as a religious penance; extended or very strict versions are demanding, and the Church exempts the young, old and ill.

quick.overview:
The Black Fast is an old form of Christian penitential fasting. Followers eat nothing until after sunset, then take a single modest meal, traditionally bread, salt, vegetables and herbs, with water allowed in the day and meat, eggs, dairy and alcohol avoided.

Its purpose is spiritual. For appearance-minded readers, the overlap is with one-meal-a-day and time-restricted eating: a single evening meal reduces the eating window and typically the calories eaten, which in other fasting research is associated with leaner body composition.
quick.how: Traditionally it is kept on fixed days such as Fridays, Ash Wednesday, Good Friday or through Lent, and sometimes on Holy Week. The evening meal is plain and meatless. Some forms also leave out liquids during the day, though many traditions allow water.
quick.risks: Going without food until evening can cause hunger, low energy, headaches and difficulty concentrating, and it is hard on anyone with diabetes, pregnancy or a history of disordered eating. The Catholic Church's current rules apply fasting only to adults roughly 18 to 59 and allow adaptations for health.

lead: The Black Fast is a strict form of Christian fasting, associated mainly with Catholic and Orthodox traditions. It means abstaining from food until after sunset and taking one modest evening meal, historically limited to bread, salt, vegetables and herbs with water, without meat, eggs, dairy or alcohol [1][2].

It was the normal form of fasting in the early Church. Wikipedia describes it as eating once a day toward evening, with nothing except a little water during the day, and notes that the meal time moved earlier over the centuries, to about 3 p.m. by the 10th century and midday by the 14th [2]. The Didache and later church councils prescribed Wednesday and Friday fasts and the forty-day Lenten fast [1][2].

In looksmaxxing discussion it is placed alongside other fasting protocols: a single evening meal makes it a form of one-meal-a-day or time-restricted eating, which people use to reduce weight and body fat. The religious meaning is penance and prayer; no published study has tested the Black Fast itself as an appearance protocol.

chain: No food until after sunset, one plain evening meal
Shorter eating window and lower calorie intake
Gradual fat loss and a leaner look
angle.text: People who adopt the fast for leanness treat it as a restricted eating window. Whatever effect on appearance arises comes through reduced overall intake, not through anything specific to the religious practice.

paras: The fast consists of abstaining from food from sunrise to sunset, followed by one modest meatless meal after dark; stricter observances also give up liquids in the day [1]. It differs from partial fasts that allow one meal at any time and from multi-day total fasts [1].

The Didache, dated around 100 AD, called for fasting on Wednesdays and Fridays, and the Apostolic Constitutions around 380 AD set a forty-day Lenten fast [1]. In 331 Athanasius urged a forty-day fast before Holy Week, and under Gregory the Great Rome kept six weeks of fasting [2].
Over time the single meal moved from after sunset to mid-afternoon and then midday, and an evening collation became common [2].

Since Paenitemini (1966) and the 1983 Code of Canon Law, fasting and abstinence are required on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday. Fasting applies from adulthood until the start of the 60th year, and on fast days one full meal and two smaller meals are allowed [2]. Episcopal conferences set local rules and may substitute other penances [2].

Fasting-minded communities mention the Black Fast as a historical precedent for one-meal-a-day eating. Its practice is primarily devotional, and observers note that it is meant for repentance rather than physical goals [1].
No studies found. Research on intermittent fasting and time-restricted eating in general exists, but the Black Fast as a religious practice has not been trialled.

timeline.event: The Didache instructs fasting on Wednesdays and Fridays [1].
